title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to measure whether inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM intent→configuration generator and an emulated execution reduces the proportion of configurations that would execute with operational faults. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification) we evaluated 72 preregistered paired intents using gpt-5-mini and a canonical deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The run completed with 144 episodes (72 pairs) and 72 model calls. All baseline executions produced no emulator-observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected-fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Because the preregistered contract used a single shared candidate per intent, the degenerate ceiling/null outcome is an expected logical consequence of the data. We archive exact execution and analysis artifacts, present representative validator traces, and provide concrete methodological recommendations for future confirmatory designs that can detect verifier utility under realistic error regimes (independent-generation arms, repair-enabled flows, adversarial task banks).

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being proposed to translate operator intents into device-level configurations for network operations (NetOps). While intent→configuration translation can speed change pipelines, generated configurations may violate reachability, security policy, or sequencing constraints and cause outages if executed without further checks. A practical mitigation in many operational proposals is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that combines stochastic LLM generation with deterministic verification and optional repair or human review. Prior work documents intent→configuration feasibility in constrained settings and prototype co-pilots that include validators [1],[2]. However, there is limited preregistered empirical evidence that quantifies whether a deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM-generated configurations that would actually execute with operational faults in an end‑to‑end emulator.

We report a preregistered paired experiment that isolates the verifier’s pure detection capability on identical generator outputs under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The central research question is: does inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM generator and emulator execution materially reduce the proportion of configurations that execute with operational faults when the identical generated candidate is evaluated both without and with verification? By design the test does not measure benefits obtainable via different generator samples or repair-enabled iterations; it measures whether deterministic detection prevents execution of candidates that would otherwise fail in the emulator.
sections.related_work: Recent studies investigate LLM-based intent→configuration translation and NetOps co-pilots [1],[3]. Multi-agent and tool-augmented frameworks integrate validators to reduce regressions [2],[4], and generate–verify–repair architectures have been examined in code and software-repair contexts [5]. Constraint‑enforcing decoding and constrained-generation methods have been proposed to reduce structured-output violations [6]. Classical deterministic network verification techniques (header-space analysis, policy checkers) provide precise invariants—reachability, ACL semantics, ordering—that make them natural verifier candidates for NetOps GVR stacks [7]. While these works motivate using verifiers together with LLMs, few supply preregistered, artifact-archived experiments that pair identical generated candidates with deterministic verification and record emulator-executed outcomes for each paired condition.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 and froze the design and analysis prior to observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational‑fault proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The confirmatory hypothesis H1 targeted an absolute paired reduction of 0.20 with two-sided alpha = 0.05 and power ≥ 0.80; the preregistered confirmatory sample was N = 72 pairs stratified across three topology-difficulty strata.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and experimental contract. Per the execution_contract, each natural‑language intent received exactly one initial LLM generation that was shared unchanged across the two paired conditions. Baseline: execute the shared candidate in an isolated emulator and record whether execution causes a fault. Guarded: run the deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) on the same candidate; if the verifier flags a violation the guarded outcome is recorded as prevented (no emulator execution); if not flagged, execute the same candidate in the emulator. This contract isolates verifier detection on identical outputs and prevents generator-sampling differences from influencing the paired comparison. Because only one shared candidate exists per intent, verifier benefit via alternative samples or repairs is impossible under this design.

Model, adapter, and verifier. The declared model is gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Provider was recorded as openai_responses and sampling parameters were recorded as temperature = null (provider default sampling semantics). Adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The canonical deterministic verifier used throughout was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = "5.0"), implementing a full_intent_constraint_validation rule set that yields a binary validity outcome plus a structured validator_trace (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after final_state mappings, violation_codes, difficulty metadata).

Task-bank construction and contamination controls. Tasks were generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and encoded as structured manifests including: natural‑language intent, required_sequence (ordered field changes), allowed_touched_fields, initial and expected final states, and difficulty labels (medium/hard/very_hard). Exact‑match contamination checks against public corpora were applied per preregistration; confirmatory pairs with exact matches would be excluded. In the executed run no confirmatory pairs were excluded (analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports zero flags).

Execution protocol and deterministic accounting. The missingness_plan allowed up to two retries for transient hosted‑API errors; retries and provider-call metadata were logged. The execution manifest reports completed_episode_count = 144 (72 pairs × 2 conditions), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 72 (one shared generation per pair). Provider-call auditing (deterministic_reconciliation.json) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, cache_miss_count = 72, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 72}.

Scoring and statistical analysis. The verifier produces per-episode binary valid/violation labels and validator_traces. The primary analysis executed paired_binary_analysis_v1 to construct the paired contingency and to run an exact McNemar two‑sided test where discordant pairs exist. We computed paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals for the paired difference with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap seed = 1729). Pre-specified subgroup confirmatory comparisons (topology complexity and policy type) were planned with Holm correction; given the observed degenerate outcome these subgroup tests were non-informative.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The experiment completed without technical failures. Representative deterministic accounting values: planned_episode_count = 144, completed_episode_count = 144, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 72. Provider-call accounting matches the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics (72 shared initial generations total).

Paired contingency and inferential outcome. Across the 72 confirmatory pairs the contingency counts are n_11 = 72, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0 (guarded × baseline). The paired estimate paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Per-condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline success_rate = 1.0 and guarded success_rate = 1.0. These numeric outputs are archived and reproducible from analysis/* artifacts.

Representative validator traces. Representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json … task-000006-*.json) show verifier parsing and validation details for shared candidates: parsed_command_count values ranged from 2 to 6, required_command_count matched task requirements, difficulty.level labels (medium/hard/very_hard) appear as specified by the task manifests, validator_version = "5.0", score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION", and violation_count = 0 for sampled examples. Validator traces include normalized_configuration strings, validation_before/after final_state mappings, and difficulty metadata; these confirm the verifier executed deterministically and did not flag violations on the generated candidates in the confirmatory bank.

Contamination, exclusions, and missingness. analysis/contamination_summary.csv records zero exact‑match contamination flags. analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 72 and zeros for failed or unscorable episodes. Because there were no exclusions or failures, sensitivity analyses treating excluded items as failures do not alter the numerical outcome in this execution.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the degenerate ceiling outcome. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics this degenerate null/ceiling outcome is a direct logical consequence of observed data: when the generator’s single shared candidate per intent causes no emulator-observed fault in the baseline, there is nothing for a verifier to detect or prevent in the guarded arm. Numerically this produces n_11 = total pairs and zero discordant cells, yielding a paired difference of 0.0 and a bootstrap CI collapsed to a point mass.

Why this outcome is scientifically informative. The run demonstrates that a preregistered paired detection test can be executed deterministically and reproducibly: the adapter produced exactly one shared generation per intent (model_calls_used = 72), the verifier executed on every shared candidate (validator traces present and archived), and emulator outcomes are recorded for both conditions. The artifact-grounded null outcome highlights that answering the broader operational question—whether verifiers reduce run-time faults in practice—requires designs that generate appreciable baseline error prevalence or permit verifier-mediated candidate changes.

Design recommendations supported by artifacts. To measure verifier utility in realistic regimes we recommend preregistered contracts (artifact-grounded) that include one or more of: (1) independent-generation arms allowing separate generator calls per condition so that verifier-triggered repair or alternate sampling can change executed candidate distribution; (2) a repair-enabled flow where the verifier, upon flagging, triggers a single deterministic repair call whose output is executed and assessed; (3) adversarial or fault-amplified task banks that intentionally include ambiguous intents and protocol edge cases to raise baseline error prevalence; (4) multi-model and sampling-parameter sweeps (temperature/headroom specified) to evaluate model and sampling sensitivity. Each proposed change is operationalizable within the existing adapter framework and would produce non-degenerate contingency tables when baseline faults are present.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: single shared generation per intent and provider-default sampling (temperature = null) were recorded but not experimentally varied; temperature = null means runtime provider defaults determined sampling behavior and remains a residual uncertainty. Construct validity: emulator-observed faults are a conservative proxy for operational harm but do not capture traffic-dependent or timing-induced emergent failures in production hardware. External validity: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini), one verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and synthetic/emulated tasks; extrapolation to other models, vendor dialects, or production devices is not supported. Conclusion validity: because baseline error prevalence was zero, the confirmatory design by construction had no power to show verifier benefit in this run.

Operational implications. The absence of baseline faults in this constrained setting suggests that, with careful prompts, dialect restriction, and deterministic task banking, modern LLMs can produce high task‑level accuracy in emulators. This should not be generalized to production operations. Deterministic verifiers remain a recommended layered control; demonstrating their operational benefit requires experiments that can produce non-negligible baseline errors or allow verifier-triggered candidate replacement or repair.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation (c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and synthetic/emulated task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator faults and the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference = 0.0, bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). This artifact-grounded null/ceiling outcome is internally consistent with the preregistered design: when identical generated candidates produce no executed faults, a verifier cannot reduce executed faults under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Future confirmatory demonstrations of verifier utility should permit independent generation, repair-enabled flows, adversarial task banks, and multi-model sampling to reveal true positive/false positive tradeoffs. All execution artifacts, validator traces, and analysis logs referenced here are archived in the evidence bundle to support replication and targeted follow-on studies.

limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation, multi‑sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: execution/model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null indicates provider default sampling semantics determined runtime sampling behavior and is a residual uncertainty recorded in the archived configuration.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
